*The page features a central, circular alchemical emblem. The border is formed by an **Ouroboros** <term>Ouroboros: An ancient symbol of a serpent eating its own tail, representing the eternal cycle of nature and the unity of the beginning and the end</term>. Within the circle, a radiant sun shines above a white **Pelican in her Piety** <term>Pelican in her Piety: A traditional motif of a mother pelican pecking her breast to feed her young with her blood, symbolizing self-sacrifice and the alchemical process of "feeding" the growing Philosopher's Stone</term>. The pelican’s nest sits atop a white cube, which is decorated with four red roses arranged in a diagonal cross.*

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page follows the title page of Jacob Böhme’s "The Three Principles of Divine Essence" (1682 edition). Having established the grand scope of his mystical cosmology on the previous page, Böhme now issues a stern spiritual warning to the reader, a common feature in seventeenth-century esoteric literature where the act of reading was seen as a potentially transformative—or dangerous—spiritual exercise.</meta>

# Necessary Warning from the Author
## to the Reader of this book / from the
## 4th Chapter, Paragraph 43, of this treatise.

But Reader / I wish to have you faithfully warned / if you are not on the path of the prodigal / and returning-to-the-Father son <note>A reference to the Biblical parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15), which Böhme uses here as a metaphor for the soul turning away from worldly desires and back toward God.</note> / then leave this my book unread / otherwise it will go ill with you. For the Grand Prince Lucifer will not rest from troubling you. For in this book he stands before the children of God entirely naked and bare. He is ashamed of this, just like a person / who is made a laughingstock before all people for the sake of their misdeeds. Therefore be warned / if your <term>the<note>original: "dz," an early modern German abbreviation for "das."</note></term> tender flesh is too dear to you / then leave my book unread. If you do not follow this / and disaster arises for you / then I wish to be innocent / blame only yourself. For what I now recognize / that I write for myself as a <term>memorial<note>original: "Memorial." Here Böhme suggests his writing serves as a personal record or a spiritual aid for his own memory, rather than a standard textbook.</note></term> / but God well knows what He wishes to do / which is still to some extent hidden from me.

<image-desc>A decorative calligraphic horizontal flourish.</image-desc>

->J. B.<-

<summary>In this preface, Jacob Böhme warns that his work is spiritually volatile and should only be read by those truly seeking a return to God, as it exposes the nature of Lucifer. He frames the writing as a personal spiritual record and disclaims responsibility for any mental or spiritual distress it may cause the "unprepared" reader.</summary>
<keywords>Jacob Böhme, spiritual warning, Lucifer, Prodigal Son, mystical insight, spiritual preparation, 17th-century theology</keywords>

The catchword "Menschen" from the previous page's footer indicates the continuation of the title of his third book.</meta>

->To the Christian<-
Reader, as will be found printed before, who will rightly consider this: Much less should he be offended by the simplicity and lowliness of the Author, since it has always pleased God according to His wise counsel to choose not what is High and Noble, Wise and Rich, etc., but rather what is low, weak, Poor, and Foolish before the world, so that He might put to shame what is High; for He raises the Poor out of the <term>dirt<note>original: "Koht." This refers to muck or dung, heightening the contrast between the author's social status and his divine inspiration.</note>, shows Grace to the Humble, and the secret of the heart is only among those who fear Him: For it is a small thing for God to make a Prophet out of a shepherd like *Amos*, or a King like *David*; out of a tax collector an Evangelist; out of unlearned fishermen like *Peter*, *James*, etc., enlightened Apostles; out of a persecutor and craftsman like *Saulus*, a <term>chosen vessel<note>original: "außerwehltes Rustzeugk." This is a direct reference to Acts 9:15, describing the Apostle Paul as a tool or vessel for God’s purpose.</note>: likewise, out of a poor, lame Shoemaker—as happened under <term>Julian the Apostate<note>original: "Juliano Apostata." A 4th-century Roman Emperor who rejected Christianity. The story mentioned here refers to a legend where a simple shoemaker's faith outperformed the wisdom of the Emperor's scholars, even moving a mountain.</note></term>—to make an intercessor and miracle-worker (who by his prayer had to move the mountain into the sea) to

Reader, it will be found printed and to be discovered [here], if one will rightly consider: Much less should he take offense at the simplicity and lowliness of the <term>Author<note>original: "Authoris." For He lifts the poor out of the <term>mire<note>original: "Koht" (modern German: Kot). Literally meaning dung or filth, used here biblically to denote a state of extreme poverty or social degradation.</note></term>, shows Grace to the humble, and the Mystery of the heart is found only among those who fear Him.

# To the Impartial Reader

-stored, everything that God has spoken through the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began, etc. Therefore, blessed is that servant who is watching when his Lord comes! In summary: let no one stumble against this **cornerstone of simplicity** <note>original: "Eckstein der Einfalt." In this context, "simplicity" refers to a humble, unpretentious faith that is often mocked by sophisticated scholars but valued by God.</note>, lest he be broken to pieces; but rather let him raise himself up by it and consider that heaven is highest where the earth is lowest, and that according to the word of the Lord <note>The transcription reads "Herzen" (heart), but this is a clear reference to the biblical prophecy in Isaiah 40:4 and Luke 3:5 regarding the "Word of the Lord."</note>, all hills and high mountains must be made low, and the valleys must be raised up, so that everywhere it may be smooth and level, and one may henceforth walk without stumbling in the **land of the living**. Praised be the LORD, the **Most High** <term>Allerhöchste|A traditional title for God emphasizing His sovereignty over human institutions</term>, who humbles this one and exalts that one, and gives his Spirit when and to whom he wills, so that no flesh may boast before him, but all the world may fear before him, and work out their **salvation** <term>Seeligkeit|A state of eternal happiness, spiritual well-being, or the soul's union with God</term> with fear and trembling. Herewith, [you are] faithfully commended to the **grace of God**.

### Hans Dieterich von Tschesch, in a missive 
### to H. P. V. H. dated Breslau 
### the 3rd of October, in the year 1641.

The philosophy and theology of Jacob Böhme is a most noble and deep foundation, universal, and extending into all things: but especially the teaching of the Three Principles <term>Three Principles|Böhme’s metaphysical system describing three realms: the dark fire-world of God's wrath, the light-world of God's love, and the physical world we inhabit</term>, which have their origin <note>original: "Uhrstandt," an archaic term for origin or primordial state</note> in the Holy Trinity / although the third principle must be properly distinguished.

I have closely examined the gift and teaching of this highly enlightened man / according to the gift that God has granted me / and found them entirely spiritual and well-distinguished / so that they are not only not offensive to any article of the Christian faith / but indeed explain them most excellently. And it is a light and a birth of this time / such as has hardly ever been opened before / explaining so precisely what God and Nature are. But just as it is a gift of God / so too is a gift of God required to recognize and understand that same light.

# PREFACE
## To the Christian, God-loving /
## Reader.

<image-desc>Large ornamental drop cap letter 'E' at the start of the first paragraph, intricately decorated with vines and scrolls in an oval frame.</image-desc>

From the 1. mother’s womb throughout the entire course of his time in this world, a person can undertake nothing more useful or necessary for himself than this: that he learns to know himself rightly: 1. What he is? 2. From what or from whom he originates? 3. For what purpose he was created? and 4. What his duty <note>original: "Ambt," referring to one's divinely appointed calling or office in life</note> is?

In such serious contemplation, he will initially 1 find how he, along with all creatures that exist, originates entirely from GOD. He will also find in all creatures 2 how he is the most noble creature among all created things. From this, he can well understand 3 how God is disposed toward him, since He made him lord over all creatures of this world, and endowed him above all creatures with sense, reason, and understanding—especially with speech—so that he can distinguish everything that makes a sound or stirs, moves, weaves <note>original: "webet," a term Böhme frequently uses to describe the pulsing, active movement of life and spirit within the universe</note>, and grows, and can judge the virtue, activity, and origin of each. And He has placed all of this into his hands, so that through his senses and reason he can master all such things, and use and direct them according to his will, as it pleases him.

Indeed, God has given 2. him an even higher and greater knowledge, so that he can look into the heart of all things to see what essence, power, and property <term>property|In Böhme’s thought, the "property" (Eigenschaft) of a thing is its specific spiritual quality or the way it manifests God's power</term> they have: whether it be in creatures, in the earth, in stones, in trees,

<margin>3.</margin> Above all this, God has given him understanding and the highest sensibility <note>original: "Sinnlichkeit," the capacity for perception and feeling</note>, so that he can recognize God his Creator—what, how, and who He may be? Also who he himself is? From what he was created and whence he came (meaning the human being), and how he is the image, essence, property, and child of the eternal, uncreated, and infinite God. How he was created out of God's essence, in which God has His own essence and property; in which He lives and reigns with His Spirit, through which God performs His works, and also loves him heartily as His own heart and essence. For whose sake He created this world along with all creatures, which for the most part could not live in such a state of being <term>state of being|original: "qualificirung," a term describing the interaction of qualities or the specific "flavor" of a thing's existence</term> without human reason and governance.

<margin>4.</margin> In this high contemplation stands Divine Wisdom <note>Often referred to as "Sophia" in this tradition, the mirror of God's glory</note> herself, and she has neither number nor end. And therein is recognized the Divine love toward man, so that man may recognize what GOD his Creator is: what He wishes to have done or left undone by him. And this is the most useful thing that man may ever fathom and seek in this world. For herein he learns to know himself—what kind of matter and essence he is, also from whence his sensibility and understanding originate, and how he was created out of God’s essence. Just as a mother gives birth to her child out of her own essence, and cares for it, and leaves all her goods to it as its own property, and makes it its possessor: thus God does with the human being, His child

# To the Christian Reader.

...child as well: He has created him and cares for him, and has made him the heir of all His goods.
<margin>Acts 17:28</margin>
In such contemplation, Divine knowledge and love toward God grow within the human being—just as between children and parents—so that the human being loves God his Father, because he recognizes that He is his Father, in whom he lives, moves, and has his being <note>The author quotes the Apostle Paul here, emphasizing the literal interconnectedness of God and humanity</note>, who cares for him and nourishes him. For thus speaks Christ, John 17:3, our brother, who was born of the Father for our salvation and sent into this world: "This is eternal life, that they might rightly recognize You, that You alone are the true GOD, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent."

<margin>5.</margin>
Since we now recognize ourselves—how we were created in God’s image, essence, and property <term>property|original: "Eigenthumb," implying both a possession and an inherent characteristic</term> out of God’s own essence—it is indeed fitting that we live in His obedience and follow Him, because He leads us as a father leads his children. We also have the promise that if we follow Him, we shall have the light of eternal life (John 8). Without this contemplation, we would all be blind and have no true knowledge of God, but would instead run along like dumb cattle, looking at ourselves and God's creation like a cow looks at a new barn door <note>A traditional German idiom (wie eine Kuh vor dem neuen Tor) describing a look of blank, uncomprehending astonishment</note>. We would set ourselves against God and His will, and live in opposition to the destruction of body and soul, and of God's noble creatures. Into such cruel and terrifying darkness we fall if we do not wish to learn to know ourselves: what we are, of what essence, and of what dignity? Whether we are eternal, or perishable with the body; or whether we must give an account <term>account|original: "Rechenschafft," a formal reckoning or audit</term> of our deeds and essence, since we were made masters of all creatures and created things, and have all of them in our power and governance.

# Preface

6. Since we then irrefutably see, know, and find that God will demand an accounting of all our deeds—how we have acted as stewards of His creatures—and since He punishes us terribly if we fall away from Him and His commandments: We have indeed seen terrifying examples of this throughout the history of the world, among Jews, Heathens, and Christians alike. We see this primarily in the example of the Great Flood, as well as in Sodom and Gomorrah; also with Pharaoh and the host of Israel in the desert, and thereafter evermore up to the present day <note>original: "biß auff dato"</note>. Thus, it is most necessary that we learn wisdom and learn to recognize ourselves—to see what great vices we carry within us and what horrible wolves <note>A metaphor for predatory sins or destructive impulses that reside within the human heart</note> are among us to resist God and His will.

7. For no human being can excuse themselves through ignorance, since God’s will is written into our very minds <term>minds|original: "Gemühte," referring to the seat of emotions, will, and conscience</term>, so that we well know what we ought to do. All of creation also bears witness against us; furthermore, we have God’s Law and Commandment, so that there is no excuse other than our own sleepy, lazy negligence. Thus, we are found to be lazy, useless servants in the Lord’s vineyard <note>A reference to the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard from Matthew 20</note>.

8. Finally, it is of the highest necessity for us that we learn to know ourselves because the Devil dwells with us in this world. He is God’s enemy and ours, who daily seduces and deceives us into falling away from God our Father, just as he did to our first parents <note>Adam and Eve</note>, so that he may increase his kingdom and deprive us of our eternal salvation; as it stands written in 1 Peter 5, verse 8:
> Your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.

9. Because we are indeed hovering in such terrifying danger in this world—surrounded by enemies on all sides and walking quite insecurely...

<summary>The author argues that self-knowledge is a moral necessity to avoid divine punishment and the deceptions of the Devil, who seeks to lead humanity away from God. He cites biblical precedents like the Great Flood and the Fall of Man as warnings against spiritual negligence.</summary>
<keywords>accountability, stewardship, Great Flood, self-knowledge, spiritual warfare, the Devil, 1 Peter 5:8, conscience</keywords>

->### To the Christian Reader.<-

[we] have in our pilgrimage <note>The "pilgrimage" refers to the traditional Christian view of earthly life as a temporary journey toward heaven</note>, and moreover carry the worst enemy within us, whom we cover up and do not wish to get to know. Yet he is the most harmful guest, who plunges us into God’s wrath: Yes, he is himself the wrath of GOD, who plunges us into the eternal fire of wrath, into eternal, unquenchable pain. It is therefore very necessary that we learn to know this same enemy well—what he is, who he is, and how he is; how he enters into us, what his rights and property within us are, as well as the Devil's right and access to us. We must know how he is befriended by our own enemy who dwells within us: how they are favorable and kind to one another, how they are both enemies of God, and how they always lie in wait for us to destroy and murder us.

<margin>10.</margin>
Furthermore, it is highly necessary for us to consider and to learn to know ourselves for these great reasons: because we see and know that because of our own enemy (who is God's enemy and ours, who dwells within us, indeed who is half of who we are <note>Refers to the "Old Adam" or the corrupt part of human nature that theologians argued must be overcome</note>), we must die and decay. If this enemy becomes powerful within us, so that he gains the upper hand and becomes the master <note>original: "Primus," meaning the first or chief</note>, he plunges us into the abyss to be with all the devils. There we would dwell forever in eternal, unquenchable torment and pain in eternal darkness. Yes, he plunges us into a house of desolation, into the eternal forgetting of all good, and into God’s aversion, so that God and all creatures become our eternal enemies.

<margin>11.</margin>
We have an even higher reason to learn to know ourselves—how we are in both good and evil—because we have the promise of eternal life. If we overcome our own enemy, along with the Devil, we shall be God's children. we shall live in His kingdom with Him, and in Him among His holy angels

impulses come, and what the good and evil within himself actually are? Also, where it originates: What truly is the origin of all good and all evil? From where or through what has evil come into the Devil and humans, as well as into all creatures? Since the Devil was a holy angel, and man was also created good, yet such discord is found in all creatures that everything bites, strikes, pushes, crushes, and is hostile to each other; and thus there is a resistance <note>original: "Wiederwille"—literally "against-will," describing a state of opposition, contrariety, or repulsion between forces</note> in all creatures, and so every body is at odds with itself. This is seen not only in living creatures, but also in the stars, elements, earth, stones, metals, leaves, grass, and wood; in all of them there is poison and malice. It is found that it must be so, for otherwise there would be no life nor mobility, nor would there be color, virtue <note>original: "Tugend"—here used in the archaic sense of an inherent power or medicinal property</note>, density or thinness, or any kind of sensation; rather, everything would be a nothingness.

<margin>14.</margin>
In such high contemplation, one finds that all of this comes from and out of God Himself, and that it is of His own essence—which He is Himself—and that He has created it thus out of Himself. Does the evil belong to formation and mobility, and the good to love, and the harsh or resistant to joy? As long as the creature is in the light of God, the wrathful or resistant element creates a rising eternal joy; but if the light of God is extinguished, it becomes an eternal rising painful torment and the hellish fire.

A Spirit, however, does nothing but ascend, flow, move, and forever give birth to itself; and primarily has three forms within its birth: namely 1. **Bitter**, 2. **Harsh**, 3. and **Heat**. And yet, these three forms are not a first, second, or third; rather, all three are only one, and each gives birth to the second and third. ### Chapter 3

The source-spirits <note>original: "Quell-geiste"; Böhme's term for the active, flowing forces or "qualities" of divine nature</note> are but a single center, wherein the fire-source rises up, and from the fire-flash comes the light; and in every source there are the first six-fold forms.

<margin>11.</margin> But mark the depth in this parable: I posit this: The harsh source in the original ground <note>original: "uhrkunde"; referring to the primal state or the "Ur-ground" of existence before manifest light</note> is the mother, out of which the other five sources—namely Bitter, Fire, Love, Tone, and Water—are born. Now these are members in their birth, and without them she [the mother] would also be nothing but an anxious, dark valley, where there would be no mobility, nor any light or life. But now that life is born within her through the igniting of the light, she rejoices in her own quality, and works upward in her own harsh quality within life; there a center then opens up again, and life is born out of her once more in a six-fold form—but now no longer in such anxiety as in the original ground, but in great joy.

<margin>12.</margin> For the source of great anxiety, which in the original ground resided in harshness before the light—and from which the bitter sting was born—is now transformed into the gentle source of love in the light from the water-spirit. And from bitterness and the sting, the source and rising of joy in the light has now come to be. Thus the fire-flash is henceforth the father of the light, and the light shines within it, and is now the sole cause of the moving birth. And the birth of love, which in the original ground was the anxious source, is now *Sul* <note>likely a reference to "Sulphur," which Böhme associates with the "soul" or the flammable principle that hosts the light</note> or the *Oleum* <note>Latin: "oil"</note>, the friendly source that penetrates through all sources, from which or out of which the light is kindled.

<margin>13.</margin> And the tone or sound in the whirling wheel <note>original: "drähenden Rade"; Böhme’s concept of the "Wheel of Nature," the perpetual motion of the divine qualities</note> is now the proclaimer or announcer in all sources, [declaring] that the beloved child is born. # Of the Three Principles

<margin>Chapter 4</margin> **Where does evil come from?** Since He alone is the Life and the Light, and the holy Power—as it is undeniably true—from where, then, does the **Wrath of God** <note>original: *Zorn Gottes*. In Böhme's system, "Wrath" is the dark, fiery potential within God that provides the energy for life but becomes "evil" when it is not balanced by Light.</note> come? Where do the Devil and his will come from, as well as the fire of Hell? From what do they take their origin? Since nothing existed before the times of the world except God alone, and He was and is a Spirit and remains so for eternity: from what was the **first matter** <note>original: *erſte materi*</note> for wickedness made? For there must have been a will within the Spirit of God to give birth to the **source-well of wrath** <note>original: *Zorn-quell*</note>. So **Reason** <term>Reason: *Vernunfft*. Thus you recognize herein the separation—how the eternal **Matrix** <term>Matrix: From the Latin for "womb," this refers to the generative, feminine principle of Nature that brings forth all forms of life and matter.</term> has a separation within itself, as mentioned earlier in Chapter 3; such is the eternal birth of the four anxieties <note>Böhme refers to the "four qualities" of the first principle: the harsh, bitter, fiery, and dark qualities that create the tension necessary for life.</note>, where between Harshness and Bitterness the Fire is born, and in the Fire-flash the Light arises; and yet each source retains its own right <note>meaning each quality maintains its specific nature and function.</note>.

<margin>10.</margin> Thus understand: when the Spirit of God moved this **Matrix**, then the **Matrix** was active; and in the igniting by the Spirit of God in the fifth form of the **Matrix**, the fiery heaven of the stars arose, which is born as a pure **Fifth Essence** <term>Fifth Essence: Known in Latin as the *Quinta Essentia* or quintessence, this is the most refined and purest element that sits above the four physical elements (earth, air, fire, water).</term>, in the fifth form of the **Matrix**, at which place the light reveals itself, from which finally the 
<margin>Sun.</margin> Sun was born. With the Sun, the **Third Principle** <term>Third Principle: In Böhme's cosmology, this is our visible, material universe, following the first (the dark world/wrath) and the second (the light world/love).</term> arose; it is now, in the **Third Principle**, the life and the "opener" in the **Matrix** of the life of all lives in this place <note>original: "loco."</note>. Just as the Heart of God in the paradisiacal heaven—in the immaterial heaven and birth—unlocks the eternal power of God, within which eternal life always arises and within which the eternal Wisdom always shines: so also the light of the Sun, which has arisen in the mute **Matrix**, unlocks the **Third Principle** of this material world through the stirring Spirit in the **Matrix**—the third and beginning **Principle**, which again takes an end in this form, and returns into its **ether** <note>original: "æther." This refers to the refined, subtle state of matter before it becomes physical or after it dissolves.</note>.

This occurred through and in the outgoing of His Spirit, which there, above the Matrix in the fifth form, fashioned the fiery heaven, just as the dear **Moses** clearly writes of it. For the Matrix is, in its original source, the **water-spirit** in the first form; and as it now became material in the place <note>original: "loco" — Latin for "place" or "region"</note> of this world, the Spirit hovered upon the water in the heavenly Matrix, which is now material, and from which the material water is born, and it formed the creatures.

In this terror, its fiery right becomes white, gentle, and mild; and this is the igniting of the light, where the fire is transformed into a white clarity.

### The Gates

<margin>18.</margin>
**P**aradise stands in the Divine Power, and is nothing bodily or tangible <note>meaning: it cannot be grasped by physical hands or the five senses.</note>; rather, its bodiliness or tangibility is like that of the Angels, where there is a bright, visible Essence, just as if it were material—and it is indeed material, but formed purely out of the Power, where everything is transparent and shining. # Divine Essence

<margin>Chapter 10</margin>
...God himself? Therein lies the purpose, the ground, and the knowledge. See, if the **will** <note>original: *Wille*</note> were in only one single essence, then the **mind** <note>original: *Gemüte*—Böhme’s term for the seat of the soul's thoughts and emotions</note> would also have only one quality to provide for the will, and it would be an unmovable thing that always lay still, doing nothing more than one single thing. In such a state, there would be no joy, no knowledge, no art, no science of more things, and there would be no wisdom. Furthermore, if that quality did not exist within the infinite, then everything would be a nothingness; there would be no mind or will toward anything, for there would be only the One.

<margin>36.</margin>
Thus, one cannot say that the whole of God, with all **three principles** <note>Böhme’s framework: 1. The dark fire-source (the Father), 2. The light-world (the Son), and 3. The outward world of nature (the Holy Spirit/manifestation)</note>, exists within a single will and essence; there is a distinction. Even though the first and third principles are not called **God** <margin>GOD.</margin>—and indeed are not God—they are nonetheless His essence, from which God's **Light** and **Heart** <note>The "Heart" refers to the Second Person of the Trinity, or Christ, the center of divine love</note> are eternally born. It is one being, much like the body and soul in a human being.

<margin>37.
1. Eternal Mind.
2. Eternal Will.
3. Eternal Heart of God.
4. Light.
5. Power.
6. Spirit.
7. Almighty God.</margin>
If the eternal **mind** did not exist, from which the eternal **will** proceeds, there would be no God. But as it is, the eternal mind exists; it gives birth to the eternal will, and the eternal will gives birth to the eternal **Heart of God**. The Heart gives birth to the **Light**, and the Light to the **Power** <note>original: *Krafft*—the active, virtuous energy of the divine</note>, and the Power to the **Spirit**, and that is the **Almighty GOD**, who exists in an unchangeable will. For if the mind no longer gave birth to the will, then the will would not give birth to the Heart, and everything would be a nothingness. But since the mind gives birth to the will, and the will the Heart, and the Heart the Light, and the Light the Power, and the Power the Spirit, the Spirit now gives birth back to the mind; for the Spirit possesses the power, and the power is the Heart, and it is an unbreakable bond.

<summary>Böhme explains that God is not a static unity but a dynamic process of eternal generation. He details how the "Almighty God" emerges through a circular chain of Mind, Will, Heart, Light, Power, and Spirit, forming an unbreakable divine bond.</summary>

# Of the Three Principles

<margin>Chapter 2.
7+</margin>
Now it is clearly evident to us that the paradisiacal fruit, which was good, was not entirely earthly; for as Moses himself says, there were two kinds: one good to eat and pleasant to look upon, and in the other lay death and fragility <note>original: *Zerbrechlichkeit*—referring to the tendency of material things to decay or break apart</note>. In the paradisiacal fruit there was no death and no fragility. But if death had been in it, then Adam would have eaten death in every fruit. Yet since no death was in it, the fruit could not be entirely earthly; although it grew out of the earth, the power of God (of the second **Principle** <term>The "Second Principle" in Böhme's philosophy represents the world of Divine Light and love</term>) was infused within it. It truly grew from the earth in the third **Principle** <term>The "Third Principle" represents the physical, material world we inhabit</term>, which God cursed after the earthly eating, so that no more paradisiacal fruit grew from the earth.

<margin>8.</margin>
Furthermore, if Adam were meant to eat earthly fruit, he would have had to eat into a body and possess intestines; then such a stench, which we now carry in our bodies, would have existed in Paradise within God’s holiness. Additionally, by eating earthly food, he would have consumed the fruit of the stars and elements, which would have immediately interacted <term>original: *inqualiret*—a term Böhme uses to describe how different qualities or forces "work into" or influence one another</term> within him, just as happened after the Fall. Also, his progeny would have grown to be like all the animals; for the animal essence <note>original: *thierische Essentia*</note> would have immediately equaled the human in power, and one stronger individual would have ruled over the others.

<margin>9+</margin>
Therefore, Adam's form was of an entirely different nature: He was a heavenly and paradisiacal man, and he was meant to eat from heavenly and paradisiacal fruit, and in that same power rule over all animals, as well as the stars and elements. Neither cold nor heat was meant to touch him; otherwise, God would have created a rough hide for him, just like all the animals, and not left him so naked.

# Of the Three Principles

<margin>Chapter 11.</margin>
<margin>30.</margin> Dear Reason <note>Böhme personifies *Vernunfft* (Reason) as the limited, earthly intellect that tries to understand divine mysteries without spiritual illumination.</note>, give up your conceit, for with this thinking and pondering you know neither GOD nor the eternal Being. How then do you hope to recognize with such a mind the likeness <note>original: *Gleichnuß*—meaning the image or representation of the divine</note> which God has brought forth out of the eternal Mind? You have often been told here that the Mind <note>original: *Gemühte*—the deep-seated seat of thoughts and emotions, often used by Böhme to describe the spiritual core of a person</note>, which is indeed the greatest essence in man, does not stand in a state of torment.

<margin>31.</margin> If we now ponder on the inclination <note>original: *Anneigligkeit*—the tendency or "leaning" of the will toward something</note>—what it was that Adam inclined toward and attracted against the prohibition, so that he should lust against God's commandment even though he was in great perfection: We find the eternal Mind, out of which Adam was also created; and because he was an extract from the eternal Mind, and from all the essences of all three Principles <note>original: *drey Principia*—the three foundational realms of existence in Böhme's cosmology: the dark fire-world (God's wrath), the light world (God's love), and the physical world</note>, he had to be tested to see if he could endure in Paradise. For the Heart of God willed that he should remain in Paradise. Now, he could not remain in Paradise unless he ate Paradisiacal fruit, and so his heart should have been entirely inclined toward God. Thus he would have lived in the Divine Center <note>original: *Göttlichen Centro*—the core of spiritual life and divine presence</note> and God would have worked in him.

<margin>32.</margin> Now, who was then against him, or who pulled him from Paradise into disobedience, so that he entered into another image?

See, you child of man: It was a threefold conflict in Adam, outside of Adam, and in everything that Adam looked upon.

If you ask: What was it? It was the three Principles: 1. The Kingdom of Hell as the power of fierceness <note>original: *Grimmigkeit*—the harsh, wrathful quality of the first principle</note> for one; and then 2. the kingdom of this world, meaning the stars and elements <note>original: *Elementa*</note>, for the other; and thirdly 3. the Kingdom of Paradise, which also wanted to have him.

<header>Of Divine Essence.</header>

<margin>Chapter 13.</margin>At this hour, his heavenly body became flesh and blood, and his strong power became bones. Then the Virgin <note>In Böhme’s writing, the "Virgin" refers to Sophia, the personification of Divine Wisdom and the spiritual counterpart Adam lost during the Fall.</note> went into her ether and shadow, but the heavenly ether <note>A subtle, spiritual substance that Böhme distinguishes from the coarse matter of the physical world.</note> entered the Principle of Power, and there she waits for all of Adam's children to see if anyone will receive her again as a bride through the new birth.

<margin>3.</margin>But what was God to do? He had created Adam out of an eternal will; since it could no longer be that Adam could have given birth to the Virgin out of himself in a Paradisiacal way, God placed the <term>Fiat</term> <note>original: *Fiat*, the Latin word for "let it be," representing the creative command or formative power of God that manifests the physical world.</note> of the great world in the middle. For Adam had now fallen back into the power of the *Fiat* as a half-broken person; because he was half-killed through his own lust and <term>imagination</term> <note>In this context, imagination refers to the soul’s power to "image" or focus its desire, which Böhme believes physically shapes our reality.</note>, God had to counsel him again if he were to live. If he were to give birth to a kingdom, there now had to be a woman, just as with all other animals for procreation. The angelic <note>original: *Englische*, which in 17th-century German means "angelic" rather than the English nationality.</note> kingdom within Adam was gone; it now had to become a kingdom of this world.

<margin>4.</margin>What then did God do with Adam? **Of the Three Principles**

<margin>Chapter 14.</margin> Now, the rising causes stirring and mobility, and the mobility causes attraction in the Will, and the Will, in turn, creates **Longing** <note>original: "Sähniligkeit"; an older form of "Sehnsucht," implying a deep, constitutive yearning</note>, so that the Will always longs for the Light; and this is an eternal bond which is without beginning and without end. For where there is a Will, there is also a Desire; and where there is a Desire, there is also an Attraction within the Will’s desire for that which the Will desires. Now, Desire is **harsh** <note>original: "herbe"; in Böhme’s system, this represents the first quality of nature—an astringent, contracting force that "cools" and "hardens" spirit into matter</note>, hard, and cold, for it draws to itself and holds fast. For where there is nothing, Desire can hold nothing; if the Will intends to hold anything, then Desire must be hard, so that the Will can grasp it. And since from eternity there was nothing, the Will could grasp and hold nothing [without this process].

<margin>62.</margin> Thus we find now that these three are an unoriginated and indissoluble bond from eternity: namely, **Longing, Willing, and Desiring**; and each one brings forth the other, and if one were not, the other would also not be—of which no one knows what it is. For in itself, it is nothing but a Spirit which in itself is in darkness, and yet it is not darkness, but rather a **Nothing**—neither darkness nor light.

Now, Longing is a craving <note>original: "Sucht"; here used not as a modern "addiction," but as a driving, infectious impulse</note>, or an infection of desire, and the Will is a **preservation** <note>original: "behältnůs"; a place of containment or a "holding-box"</note> within desire. If the Will is to hold it, it must become **graspable** <note>original: "faßlich"; both "comprehensible" and "tangible"</note>, and it must not be one thing in the will, but two. If there are then two, the **Attraction** must be the third, which draws the graspable into the will. Since this has been so from eternity, it is found that from eternity there is a **laboring** <note>original: "quällen"; a central word for Böhme that combines the idea of a "source-fountain" (Quelle) with "torment" or "labor" (Qual). It describes the agonizing birth of existence.</note> and motion; for that which is grasped must labor and be something, so that the Will can grasp something; then, since that same "something" exists, it must be **Harsh** and attractive, so that it [leads] to...

<margin>Chapter 14.</margin> ...becomes something. When it is then harsh <note>original: "herbe"; in Böhme’s system, this represents the first quality of nature—an astringent, contracting force that "cools" and "hardens" spirit into matter</note> and attractive, this attraction creates something tangible <note>original: "begreifliches"; literally something that can be grasped or comprehended</note>, so that the Will has something to seize and to hold. And when it is thus tangible, it is thicker than the Will, and it shadows the Will, and covers it; and the Will is inside it, and Longing <note>original: "Sähnen"</note> creates them both. Now, when the Will is within that which is tangible, then the tangible thing is the Will's darkness, for it has encompassed the Will with its tangibility. Now the Will cannot escape from the tangible, and yet it always longs for the Light, so that it might be delivered from the darkness—which it nevertheless creates for itself through its own longing and attraction.

<margin>63.</margin> From this arises anxiety <note>original: "ängstlichkeit"; for Böhme, this refers to a cosmic state of "narrowness" or "compression" (related to the Latin *angustia*) that forces a breakthrough</note>, because the Will is locked in darkness; and the attraction of the Will creates mobility, and this mobility causes the Will to rise up out of the darkness. Now, this rising is the first **Essence** <note>original: "Essentia"; the fundamental substance or being</note>, for it is born within the attraction and is itself the attraction. Now the Will also cannot endure this attraction, for it makes the Will dark with the essence it has drawn in, which the Will grasps; thus the Will resists it, and this resistance is the stirring <note>original: "rügen"; an archaic term for movement or agitation</note>, and this stirring causes a separation or a breaking apart within what has been drawn in, for it divides things. The harshness within the attraction cannot tolerate this either, and the anxiety within the Will grows greater, and the attraction—trying to hold onto the stirring—also grows greater. And when the stirring is thus pulled so hard and held by the harsh attraction, it compresses itself and becomes prickly, and it stings within the harsh anxiety. Then the harshness draws itself in even more forcefully; at that point, the sting becomes so great within the anxiety that the Will erupts terrifyingly <note>original: "schrecklich"; also implying a sudden "shock" or "startle"</note> and sets its purpose to escape from the darkness.

# Of the Three Principles

<margin>Chapter 15. 12.</margin> Because His [God's] will was to also have creatures within this throne in the eternal Element <note>In Böhme’s theology, the "Element" (singular) is the pure, spiritual substance of the heavenly world, distinct from the four earthly elements.</note> who would take the place of the fallen Devil and represent that place <note>original: "locum"</note> in Heaven in Paradise, He created Man out of the Element.

<margin>13.</margin> And as this **place** <note>original: "locus"</note> was now twofold—and with the eternal **original source** <term>uhrkunde</term> <note>original: "uhrkunde"; Böhme uses this to mean the primordial foundation or the "original record" of all things</note> threefold—the first **Principle** <note>original: "Principium"</note> existed in the great anxiety [of the dark world]. And then the second **Principle** existed in the Divine Delight in Paradise. And then the third **Principle** existed in the light of the sun, and in the quality of the stars and elements: so Man also had to be created out of all three. This was so that he might be an angel in this **place** <note>original: "loco"</note> and receive all knowledge and understanding, so that he could also have eternal joy with the figures and images which do not stand in the eternal spirit, but in the eternal figure, just as all things are in this world.

Otherwise, if it were from the spirit, it would also discern the beginning of all things, just like man, who catches and distinguishes all things through the sound he hears.

14. 15. If it is tolerable, the feeling gives it into the heart before the **flash of life**, and the will of the mind gazes further into the thing to a great depth, seeing what is within it and how much of that thing it wishes to accept and let in. When it is enough, the will then gives it to the spirit of the soul, as to the **eternal colonel** <note>original: "Obristen"; the highest commanding officer or chief</note>, who leads it out from the heart with his strong and rigorous power in the resonance, onto the **tong-** <note>catchword for the next page: "Zunge" (tongue)</note>

18. Thirdly, the third **Rule** <term>Regiment; the governing influence of the external, material world</term> arrives for the formation of the **Word**: the spirit of the stars and elements. It mixes itself into the housing and senses of the **Mind** <term>Gemüht; the seat of emotions and will</term> and wishes to form the **Word** out of its own power. # Of the Three Principles

# The XVII. Chapter.

## Concerning the terrible, lamentable, and wretched Fall of Adam and Eve in Paradise.

### The Mirror of Humanity.

1. If the gates of the deep were not opened within my **mind** <term>mind; *Gemühte*, Böhme’s term for the seat of the soul’s will, desires, and inner disposition</term>, so that I could see what the opposition against God’s kingdom is: then I would also think it was merely a matter of disobedience, and of a bite of an apple, as the text in Moses simply passes over it: although Moses writes quite correctly. <note>Böhme suggests that while the biblical account of Genesis is true, it contains a deeper, hidden meaning about the nature of reality that isn't immediately obvious from a literal reading.</note>

2. For it was a matter of earthly eating and drinking: by which the Paradisiacal man was captured by the spirit of this world, which now **works within** <term>works within; *inqualiret*, a term Böhme uses to describe how a quality, spirit, or force permeates and operates within a substance</term> all people. Holy Scripture and reason also testify to this, that man is not at home in the elemental kingdom of this world.
<margin>John 18:36.</margin>
For Christ says: My kingdom is not of this world.
<margin>John 15:19.</margin>
And to his Apostles he says: I have called you out of this world:
<margin>1 Cor. 15:50.</margin>
Likewise <note>original: "Item", a Latin term commonly used in early modern German texts to mean "likewise" or "furthermore"</note>, flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God.

3. Also, we see that the kingdom of this world dies away and breaks apart from man. Since Adam bore the **image** <term>image; *Bildnuß*, the spiritual form or "likeness" of God that Böhme believes was man’s original, eternal body</term> of the kingdom of God, which was eternally unbreakable and stood in Paradise; we can therefore say with no basis that he bore the image of the kingdom of this world, for this world is transitory and breakable: but the image in Adam was imperishable and unbreakable.

<summary>Böhme introduces the Fall of Adam and Eve, arguing that it was not merely a simple act of disobedience but a metaphysical transformation where humanity became enslaved to the earthly "spirit of this world." He emphasizes that man's original, eternal nature (the divine image) is fundamentally different from his current, perishable physical existence.</summary>

### Of the Divine Essence

<margin>Chapter 17.</margin>
...[he] became lustful through the spirit of this world, desiring to mix himself with the four elements. Thus the commandment came and spoke: "You shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil."

Now, the knowledge of good and evil is certainly not manifest in Paradise or the Kingdom of Heaven, but only in the departure from the <term>Element; the single, pure spiritual substance</term> into the <term>Wrath; "Grimm," the harsh, dark, or destructive quality of nature</term>. There, the knowledge of evil stands revealed on its own; there, the <term>Essences; the fundamental spiritual qualities or "beingness" of a thing</term> are alone combustible, and death is hidden within them—concerning which God said: "When you eat of it, you shall die the death."

<margin>17.</margin>
God meant the body which he would receive from the infection of the four elements; it would have to die. ## Of the Three Principles

<margin>Chapter 17.</margin>
God created man out of the <term>clod of earth; "Erden-kloß," referring to the crude, material substance</term>, so that his veil might be before his face, so that the earthly man should not look into God's face. To be sure, he became a clod of earth and mere earth when he ate the earthly fruit, which God had forbidden him. Had Adam been earthly on earth before the Fall, God would not have forbidden him the earthly fruit; furthermore, if he had been created from the earth’s element, why did the earthly element not immediately clothe him with a rough skin? Why did it leave man naked and bare? And even though it had already taken possession of him, it still left him naked and bare.

<margin>21.</margin>
Only Moses speaks of the tablet of God, which was engraved through with the Ten Commandments, so that one can see through them into Paradise; he hangs the <term>veil; "Deckel," referring to the veil Moses wore to hide the radiance of God's glory</term> before his face, as is seen with the people of Israel. Because man has become earthly, he must cast off the earthly again; <margin>Exodus 34:33 & 35.</margin> then he shall go with Joshua and Jesus <note>In German, these names are linguistically linked; Joshua is seen as a "type" or precursor to Jesus leading his people to the promised land.</note> into the promised land of Paradise, and not remain with Moses in the wilderness of this world, where the veil of this world hangs before Paradise.

<margin>22.</margin>
Let no human reason allow itself to imagine that God made any animal out of a clod of earth, as a potter makes a pot; rather, He spoke: "Let all kinds of animals come forth, each according to its kind." That is, out of all <term>Essences; the inner living qualities of things</term>, each according to the property of its own essence. Thus it was also figured through the <term>Fiat; the divine creative word, from the Latin "let it be"</term> out of its own essence; so also were all trees, herbs, and grasses, all at once together. How then would the image of God have been made from fragile essences? Since it was created in Paradise out of the Eternal.

### The Gates of Great Sins and Aversion Against GOD through Man.

<margin>70.</margin> If we consider the abomination and great sins before God in man, which our first parents bequeathed to us as an inheritance, then we might never become joyful in this world, if the spirit of this world did not plunge us into a foolish, illusory joy <note>original: *spiegel-fechter frewde*; literally "mirror-fencer’s joy," referring to shadow-boxing or a happiness that has no substance.</note> in our prison: Or if the rebirth did not so often highly gladden us with the prospect of being released from this prison. For we find in this life nothing but pure abomination, sin, distress, and death, and we hardly attain a glimpse of eternal joy in this life.

<margin>71.</margin> Now the mind <term>Gemühte; the deep-seated disposition of the soul where thoughts and desires originate</term> asks: What then is sin? Why does God have a loathing for the being he has created? See, you child of man: before God there is no sin in heaven; sin is in you alone, and sins separate us and our God from one another. Otherwise everything is fixed <note>original: *fix*; an alchemical term for a substance that is stable and resists change, here meaning a state that is established and consistent with its own nature.</note> and good in its own being; the kingdom of hell and of wrath is good in itself according to its own region; it lays for itself—

## Of the Three Principles

<margin>Chapter 17.</margin>
...[n itself, but it] feels no torment <note>original: *Marter*</note> or woe; rather, its world is its birth and the rising of its agony <note>original: *Quahl*</note>, and it desires nothing else.

72. Thus the kingdom of this world is also in itself fine and good; it also feels no woe, but the stirring of the elements—such as the ignition <note>original: *Anzündens*; an alchemical term for the spark of life or energetic activation</note>, the heat, cold, air, and water—is its growth and flourishing, and it causes itself no pain: it also has no trembling or fear within itself.

73. Only man, who has come forth from another principle <note>original: *Principio*</note>, experiences woe, distress, lamentation, and trembling in these two principles, for he is not in his fatherland, and neither of these two principles <note>original: *Principia*</note> can reach his fatherland. Therefore, the poor soul must so squeeze and press itself that it reaches its fatherland again; it must go again through the gates of the deep agony of death; it must burst open two kingdoms, and is stuck here between the door and the hinge <note>original: *zwischen Thür und Angel*; an idiom for being caught in a painful, transitional squeeze or a moment of crisis</note>, and is always infected by those things that hold it back and squeeze it greatly; it is stuck as if in a press.

74. If it presses toward God, the Devil holds it on one side by a bond, and the world on the other bond, and they strike at it; the Devil ignites it with fury <note>original: *Grimm*</note> and wrath—this is a sin that cannot reach the Kingdom of God. And the world leads it into pride <term>Hoffahrt; an archaic term for excessive, haughty pride or vanity</term>, greed, and the lust of the flesh, so that the soul's essences <term>Essentien; the fundamental spiritual substances or energies that comprise the soul</term> become full of the fleshly will. For the will of the mind <term>Gemüht; the deep-seated disposition of the soul where thoughts and desires originate</term> draws these things into the soul, and so the soul becomes entirely impure, swollen, and dark from what has been drawn in, and cannot reach the Light of God. # Of the Divine Essence

<margin>Chapter 17.</margin>
...[The soul does] not [fit] within it. Only the gates of the deep <note>original: *Thoren der Tieffe*; referring to the spiritual threshold between the light and dark worlds</note> must be burst open, so that the essences <term>essences: spiritual substances or energetic powers that constitute reality</term> press into freedom out of the darkness. But if the mind <note>original: *Gemüte*; the inner disposition or seat of consciousness</note> is filled [with worldly things], it cannot do so; then there begins terror, fear, hesitation, and despairing of the Kingdom of God, which causes the soul nothing but pure agony <note>original: *Quahl*</note>.

<margin>75.</margin>
You should also know how it is a sin before God: you have within you the Element <term>the Element: in Böhme’s theology, this is the "holy element" or the spiritual atmosphere of heaven, distinct from the four physical elements</term>, which is a delight for God. If you then rage and storm with the agony of hell, you touch the Element and awaken the wrath <note>original: *Grimm*; a technical term for the dark, fiery, and judgmental aspect of God's first principle</note> to go forth. You do exactly what the Devil did when he stirred up and ignited the wrath in the *Fiat* <note>original: *Fiat*; the creative 'Let there be' command</note>, from which the wrath brought forth the earth and stones. You sin all the way into heaven before God. <margin>Isaiah 7:13</margin> Regarding this, the prophets complained in many places that the disobedient people offended their God; although it does not cause Him pain within Himself, His wrath is nonetheless ignited according to the first principle <note>original: *Principio*</note> in the gates of the deep wherein the soul stands, and it is a pure abomination before Him.

<margin>76.</margin>
See, everything you let into your mind—if your soul is not inclined toward God so that it stands upon Him in faith and confidence—then everything you do is sin to you. For you lead an earthly mind into the gates of the deep where the Spirit of God moves, and you defile the Element which is before God.

<margin>77.</margin>
You might say, "How? God dwells in heaven!" O you blind mind, full of darkness! The heaven where God dwells is also in you, just as Adam was in Paradise while on earth. Do not let the Antichrist <note>Böhme often uses "Antichrist" to refer to institutional religious authorities who mislead the faithful about the nature of God</note> point you outside this world beyond the stars. He lies like the Devil himself. God is everywhere! The foundation of hell is also everywhere, as the prophet David says:

...if you are inclined, whether you are inclined toward *righteousness*, *love*, *faithfulness*, and *truth*: *likewise* <note>original: *Item*</note>, toward *chastity*, *discipline*, and *mercy*, then it is well with you, and it is good! But where this is not the case, reach into your breast and confront your fleshly heart and examine it; gather your senses together into a prison, and press upon your fleshly heart so that the *elements* <note>original: *Elementa*</note> within you tremble. The flattering and lying devil, who has seated himself in your fleshly heart, will surely yield when he feels these blows which do not taste sweet to him; you will indeed become differently minded. This is not composed by an unpracticed mind <note>original: *Gemühte*; the seat of the will and inner disposition</note>; it has experienced it itself; therefore, let it stand as a *memorial* and a constant exhortation. <margin>80.</margin>
When *Adam* and his wife had eaten of the earthly fruit, they were ashamed before one another, for they became aware of the animal organs <note>original: *Thierischen Glieder*</note> of their body for procreation <term>procreation: Böhme posits that before the Fall, humans did not reproduce through animal-like sexual organs, but through a spiritual, heavenly process</term>, and they broke off shrubs and held them over their shame <note>original: *Schahm*; refers both to the feeling of shame and the private parts</note>: And the voice of God walked in the garden, high within their mind, and they hid themselves behind the trees in the garden.

<margin>81.</margin>
Here we clearly see and indeed grasp that God in the beginning had not created such an image with animal organs for procreation. For what God creates for eternity, for that there is no shame. Also, they only then became aware that they were naked; the *elements* had possessed them and they had put on no clothing—nor could they—for man’s spirit was not of the *essences* <note>original: *Essentien*</note> and property of the *elements*, but from the Eternal.

<margin>82.</margin>
And in this place, nothing is more tangible than to see and recognize that *Adam*, before his sleep and before his wife, had no animal form.

...Tincture <note>An alchemical and theosophical term for the subtle, animating spirit or "dye" that gives life and quality to matter</note>, so that the Light of Life is extinguished: then the body falls away as a dead carcass. Likewise, regarding the Water, if the Tincture ignites itself in meekness <note>original: *Sanfftmuht*; the gentle, light-filled quality of God</note>, it becomes fat, thick, and swollen, entirely diseased, also dark and murky, in which the flash of life moves like a prickling thorn. And thus the life of man is surrounded on all sides by enemies, and the poor soul is always surrounded by many chains in a heavy prison, and always fears that when the body breaks, it might fall back home to the Executioner, the Devil, in his kingdom.

Had he done so, the torment of darkness in its wrath <note>original: *Grimm*; the fierce, dark, and foundational "fire" of God's nature</note> would not have stirred him; instead, he would have remained a Conquering Prince in the triumph of Paradise, over the kingdoms of hell and of this world.

# Of the Three Principles

<header>Of the Three Principles</header>

Chapter 17. ...the soul [took] the swollen kingdom of the <term>outbirth: *Außgebuhrt*; the external, material world that "grew out" of the spiritual realm</term> into its own will; thus the pure paradisiacal soul became dark. The element of the body then seized the human, or the <term>massa: the raw material or physical "lump" of man</term>, which pulled the will of the soul and the mind into the element. In this way, he became a fleshy human and received the <term>wrath: *Grimm*; the fierce, consuming fire of God’s first principle</term>, which turned the strong breakthrough in the Gates of the Deep <note>The spiritual boundary where light and darkness meet</note> toward God into hard bones and skeletal remains.

88. And it is for us a excellent and high thing to recognize: for it is seen in the Light of Life how the marrow in the bones possesses the noblest and highest <term>Tincture: a subtle, animating spiritual essence</term>, wherein the spirit is sweetest and the light is brightest. This may be recognized in fire <note>Böhme often uses the physical behavior of fire and light as a map for spiritual truths</note>, unless you are otherwise blind with contradiction; and it is sharply recognized that these paths, where the hard bones are now, were once **miraculous power**, which shattered the Gates of Darkness, in which the angelic human stood within the Light.

89. Therefore, when Adam fell into the <term>infatuation: *Sucht*; a state of diseased longing or passion for the material world</term>, Divine Providence surrounded this power and strength with the might of the **First Principle** <note>The "First Principle" represents God's strict, fiery potential and righteous severity</note>—the rigorous power of God’s sharpness—so that the torments of the first and third principles should not so easily touch him. And this occurred during Adam’s sleep, when God built Adam for this world, of which <margin>1 Cor. 15:45.</margin> Saint Paul also speaks: that the natural man was created into a fragile life. This happened during the temptation of Adam, at the time when God made his natural wife out of him. Before that, however, he was a **heavenly image**, and he must become this again at his return on the Last Day.

90. And even if the Devil and this world should rage against it, this is the ground of truth, recognized high within the wonders of God, and not born of trifles or mere opinion.

<header>Of the Three Principles</header>

<margin>Chapter 17.</margin>...said: "Who told you that you are naked? Have you not eaten of the tree of which I told you that you should not eat?" And he spoke: **"The woman gave to me, and I ate of it."** And He spoke to the woman: **"Why did you do that?"** And she spoke: **"The serpent deceived me, so that I ate."**

<margin>92.</margin> Here one sees quite clearly how the Devil had lost his angelic <note>original: *Englische*; Böhme uses this to mean "angel-like" or belonging to the state of an angel</note> image, and now comes in the form of a serpent with his murderous lies and deceives the woman. Because he had not been able to completely fell Adam, he beset the woman and promised her cleverness and the riches of this world—that they would be within them just like God.

The Devil mixed lies and truth together and said: **"They would be as GOD."** But he meant this according to the <term>first Principle: in Böhme's system, this is the "Dark World" or the foundation of fire and wrath, separated from God’s Light</term> of Wrath, and he left Paradise out of the equation. Eve <note>original: *Heva*</note>, however, understood it to mean she would remain in Paradise in Divine delight.

<margin>John 8:44</margin>
<margin>93.</margin> Therefore it is not good to chat with the Devil; he is a murderer and a liar from the beginning of his kingdom, and a thief as well. He comes only because he wants to murder and steal, as seen here. ## Of the Entrance of Holy Souls to GOD, and of the Entrance of Godless Souls into Destruction.

### The Gates of the Body’s Breaking from the Soul.

1. Suggests being stripped bare of all earthly or astral coverings, remaining only in the spiritual "raw" state.</note> and is no longer seen by any human; instead, the deep **abyss** without end or number is its dwelling house. And its works, which it performed here—
<margin>Revelation 14:13.</margin> stand as images in its **tincture** <term>Tinctur: the spiritual "dye" or essence that retains the permanent record of a person's character and deeds.</term> and follow after it.

# **The Divine Essence**

<margin>Chapter 19. 45.</margin>
But what shall I write of you, you earthly Babylon <note>original: "Ba-bel." For Böhme, Babylon represents the state of spiritual confusion and the false, external church that prioritizes power and ritual over inner transformation.</note>? I must nonetheless show you the foundation <note>original: "Grund."</note>, so that your hypocrisy <note>original: "Gleißnerey."</note> may be brought to the light, and so the devil does not stand there in the form of an angel, acting as a god within man in the lustful kingdom of this world—for that is his highest ambition.

<margin>46.</margin>
Look, you call yourself a Christian and boast of being a child of God; indeed, you confess this with your mouth, but your heart is a murderer and a thief. You strive only for worldly honor and riches, and you do not consult your conscience about how you might obtain them. You occasionally intend to enter into earnest repentance <term>repentance; original: "Busse," meaning a deep inner turning away from the self and toward God</term>, but the devil holds you so that you cannot. You say: "Tomorrow," and that delay lasts forever. You think: "If only my chests were full, then I would become a pious person; if I only had enough beforehand so that I would not want for anything later." You persist in this until your end, which the devil paints for you as being far off.

<margin>47.</margin>
In the meantime, you consume the sweat and blood of the wretched, and you gather all their distress and lamentation into your soul. You take their sweat and use it to drive your pride <note>original: "Hoffahrt."</note>, yet your actions must be held as holy. You offend the wretched so that they, through your example and conduct, also become reckless and do what is wrong before God. They curse you and are thereby also ruined, and thus abomination is born from abomination. But you are the primary cause; and even if you present yourself ever so elegantly and wisely, the driver <note>The "driver" or "oppressor" is a recurring Böhme image for the ego or the demonic influence that pushes the soul toward sin.</note> is always before you, and you are the root of all sins.

<margin>48.</margin>

<summary>Böhme delivers a scathing critique of religious hypocrisy, warning that those who prioritize worldly wealth and pride over true repentance are servants of the devil, despite their outward Christian claims. He identifies the exploitation of the poor as a root cause of spiritual corruption for both the oppressor and the oppressed.</summary>

# **Of the Three Principles**

<margin>Chapter 19.</margin> [The soul clings to the] thread and will not let go, yet her essences still stick fast in God’s wrath; the torment of gross sins plagues them, and the thread of faith of the **New Birth** <term>New Birth; original: "Newen-gebuhrt," the central spiritual transformation in Böhme's theology</term> is very weak. One must now penetrate to God through the gates of the deep, through the suffering and death of Christ, and through the kingdom of hell; yet hell still has a great bond upon the soul, and the falsehood has not yet been washed away.

<margin>42.</margin> Then the **Bridegroom** <note>Christ, often depicted as the soul's spouse in mystical tradition</note> says: "Come!" But the poor soul says: "I cannot yet; my lamp is not yet adorned." Nevertheless, she holds the Savior by the thread and further directs her **imagination** <term>imagination; in Böhme's view, this is the soul's power to "image" or shape its internal reality</term> through the thread of faith and confidence into the heart of God, until she is finally **ransomed** <note>original: "rantioniret," from the French "rançonner"</note> out of the **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction; an alchemical term for the necessary decay or purging of the old, corrupt nature</term> through the suffering of Christ.

<margin>43.</margin> But as for what their putrefaction is, my soul does not desire to share it with them; for it is their own horrible sins, ignited in the wrath of God. There the poor soul must bathe until she enters into rest through her small faith; yet her transfiguration will never equal that of the truly-born saints in eternity. Even though they are indeed redeemed out of hell and enjoy heavenly joy, the greatest joy is found in the earnest **regeneration** <note>original: "Wiedergeburt"</note>, in which **Paradise**, power, and wonders arise.

<margin>44.</margin> And your worldly pomp and glory, beauty, and wealth will not exalt you before God as you imagine. Your office held here—whether you were a **king** or a **priest**—will also not do it; you must be born anew through the Savior if you wish to be beautiful in heaven. You must lead others toward righteousness, and then you will shine before God with your office like the splendor of the heavens, and your works will follow you. O man, reflect upon this!

<summary>This page describes the soul's arduous journey toward God, clinging to a "thread of faith" to escape the decay of sin and the wrath of God. Böhme emphasizes that true heavenly glory comes from inner spiritual rebirth rather than earthly status or titles.</summary>

# **Of the Divine Essence**

<margin>Chapter 19. Par. 45.</margin>
But what shall I write of you, you **earthly Babylon** <term>Babylon; for Böhme, this signifies the "false" church and the corrupt social order that values outward form and power over inner spiritual truth</term>? I must nonetheless show you the foundation, so that your **hypocrisy** <term>hypocrisy; original: "Gleißnerey," literally "glimmering," referring to a deceptive outward appearance of holiness</term> may be brought to the light, and so the **Devil** does not stand there in the form of an angel and remain a god within man in the lustful kingdom of this world—as that is his highest ambition.

<margin>46.</margin>
See, you call yourself a Christian and boast of being a child of God; you confess this indeed with your mouth, but your heart is a murderer and a thief. You strive only for worldly honor and riches, and your conscience does not care how you might acquire them. You intend, perhaps, to enter into **earnest repentance** <term>earnest repentance; "ernste Busse," a central concept for Böhme involving a total, painful turning of the soul’s will back toward God</term> one day, but the Devil holds you so that you cannot. You say: "Tomorrow," and that "tomorrow" lasts forever. You think: "If only my chests were full, then I would become a pious person; if I only had enough first, so that I would not suffer lack later." You carry on this way until your end, which the Devil paints as being far off in the distance.

<margin>47.</margin>
Meanwhile, you consume the sweat and blood of the miserable, and you gather all their distress and complaints into your own soul. You take their sweat and use it to fuel your **pride** <note>original: "Hoffahrt," meaning high-living or arrogance</note>, and yet your actions must be regarded as holy. You offend the wretched man, so that through you and your behavior, he too becomes reckless and does what is wrong before God. He curses you and ruins himself thereby, and so **abomination is born from abomination**; but you are the primary cause. And though you present yourself so elegantly and wisely, the **driver** <note>original: "Treiber," referring to a taskmaster or an inner demonic driving force</note> is always before you, and you are the root of all sins.

<margin>48.</margin>
Even when you pray, you wear your dark garment, which is defiled with vain vices: with usury, greed, pride, unchastity, fornication, anger, envy, and theft.

<summary>In this passage, Böhme delivers a scathing critique of "Babylon," accusing self-proclaimed Christians of hypocrisy and the economic exploitation of the poor. He warns that delaying spiritual repentance in favor of accumulating wealth allows the Devil to rule the soul under a mask of piety.</summary>

<margin>52.</margin>
Human intercession reaches only so far as the soul hangs upon the **thread of rebirth** <note>original: "Fadem der Wiedergeburt"; Böhme uses this to describe the tenuous but vital spiritual connection a struggling soul maintains with God's grace</note>, and is not entirely a worm or a beast. It reaches as far as the soul penetrates toward God with desire. If those praying are true Christians who earnestly stand in the new birth, their **soul-spirit** <note>original: "Seelen-geist"; the higher, spiritual aspect of the soul that can communicate with the divine realm</note>—on the thread of the bond of poor souls—penetrates toward God along with the poor soul in its fervent love for it. In this way, it certainly helps the poor imprisoned soul in its struggle to burst the chains of the devil.

This occurs especially before the departure of the poor soul from the body, and particularly through the prayers of parents for children, or siblings, or blood-relatives. For in such cases, their <term>tinctures</term> <note>original: "Tincturen"; in Böhme's alchemy-influenced theology, these are the essential spiritual qualities or "life-liquids" that carry the soul's power</note> <term>inter-qualify</term> <note>original: "inqualiren"; a technical term meaning to work together or influence one another by sharing the same qualities or essence</note>, as they are born of one blood. In this great struggle, the spirit goes much more willingly and achieves victory more easily and powerfully than a stranger's spirit, provided they stand in the new birth. But without this, nothing is obtained; no devil can break another.

<margin>53.</margin>
However, if the soul of the dying is entirely loosed from the bond of Jesus Christ and does not reach the thread itself through its own penetration, then the prayer of those standing around helps not at all. Instead, it happens to them as Christ said to his seventy disciples in Matthew 10:12, whom he sent out: "When you go into a house, greet it; and if a child of peace is in such a house, your greeting of peace shall rest upon it; if not, your greeting of peace shall return to you again." Thus, the heartfelt wish of love and the earnest penetration toward God remain with the believers once more.

<summary>Böhme explains that intercessory prayer is effective only if the recipient still has a spiritual connection to God, highlighting that blood relatives have a unique spiritual advantage in helping a soul fight the devil's influence. He concludes that prayer offered for an unreachable soul is not wasted but returns to the person who prayed.</summary>

<margin>Chapter 20. 5.</margin>
When God the Lord had pronounced the **sentence** <note>original: "Sententz"; referring to the divine judgment or decree following the Fall</note> upon Adam and Eve because of their earthly misery, as well as the toil, sorrow, and heavy burden they would have to carry; and when He confirmed them as man and wife, bound in marital duty to cling to one another as one body, and to love and help each other as a body does its own members; they were then entirely naked and bare. They stood there and were ashamed of their earthly image, and especially of the members of their shame, as well as the evacuation of earthly food from their bodies. For they saw that, according to the external body, they now possessed an **animal nature** <note>original: "Thierische Ahrt"; Böhme emphasizes that the Fall transformed the human body from a luminous, spiritual substance into a biological, animalistic one</note> in every way. Heat and cold also fell upon them, and the modest image of God was lost; and they were now to propagate themselves in the manner of animals.

<margin>6.</margin>

He also taught them how they should seek and reveal the **wonders** within the spirit of this world, and how to clothe themselves from those wonders.

<margin>7.</margin>

### Divine Essence. Chapter 20.

A golden radiance comes trotting in high and proud; it glitters on all sides. Everyone says: "It is blessed," for it adorns itself most beautifully. It sets its throne above the hills and mountains. Everyone greets it. It draws the **Tincture of the Earth** <term>Tincture: In Böhme’s mystical alchemy, the "Tincture" is the hidden spiritual life-force or "quintessence" that gives value and beauty to material things like gold.</term> to itself so that it alone might glitter. It robs the **Kingdom of Christ** of its temporal bread; it devours the sweat of the miserable person and says to him: "You are mine, I am your God, I place you as I will. You are the dog at my feet; if I do not want you, I hunt you out of my house; you must do what I want." And the poor little creature <note>original: "elende Thierlein"; Böhme often uses this diminutive to emphasize the vulnerability and "beastly" or animal-like nature of the human soul when it is stripped of divine grace.</note> must say: "I am indeed your miserable servant, only spare me."

And when the sweat of his brow <note>original: "Schweiß seiner Nasen" (sweat of his nose); a literal rendering of the German idiom for hard labor, referencing the curse of Adam in Genesis 3:19.</note> presses him so that it hurts him, consuming his heart, then he becomes impatient with his master and curses him, seeking the way of lies and deceit to see how he might make the heavy burden lighter.

<margin>33.</margin>
When his heart finds him so unjust, it strikes him and takes away his "false bread"—that which he intended to eat under a gentle yoke—and it strangles him most cruelly, leaving him no time to escape. He, however, remains full of impatience under the heavy yoke, grunting and murmuring, seeking every false escape to lighten his burden so that he might eat his bread in peace. But it will not be; the driver <note>The "driver" (Treiber) represents the relentless force of the Law or the "fierce" principle of nature that pursues the conscience of the sinner.</note> is behind him and takes his bread, feeding him with misery under his yoke.
